current_answer: The early-career AI warning just met a serious counter-signal. Three U.S. exposure studies find weaker hiring, employment or initial earnings for young people in more exposed work. A new population-wide Norwegian study finds negative but statistically non-robust estimates for workers aged 22–25, and its backdated placebo tests can be larger than the post-ChatGPT effect. That does not erase the U.S. pattern: the countries, labor markets, data and methods differ, and neither side observes a clean employer-by-employer AI rollout. The honest verdict is harder: entry routes may be tightening in some settings, but there is no universal, causal AI job-loss finding yet.

catalogue_card.question: Did AI really squeeze young workers out of work?
catalogue_card.text: A Norwegian population study finds no robust young-worker displacement. The U.S. warning is real, but it is no longer a universal story.

summary: A Norwegian CESifo working paper uses population-wide employer-employee records from 2015 through March 2025 and finds no robust statistically significant employment displacement among ages 22–25 in highly generative-AI-exposed occupations.

Its young-worker estimates are negative but statistically insignificant across three designs. Backdated placebo estimates can be larger, warning that apparent post-ChatGPT decline may partly be a secular trend.

Three U.S. exposure studies still report weaker early-career hiring, employment or initial earnings, and the revised Stanford payroll analysis reports a 19% relative gap for ages 22–25. Those findings remain descriptive or associational rather than adoption-based causal estimates.

An EIB firm study reports no adverse employment effect in its instrumented broad-AI adoption model. It covers 2019–2024, broadly defined AI and firm headcount, so it does not settle generative-AI entry routes.
A Federal Reserve analysis still finds little distinct AI-driven decline in broad U.S. job postings. Postings are not realized hires, and a broad result does not erase a narrow one.
uncertainty: No current study can tell a reader whether their own job will be lost to AI.

The U.S. early-career findings are exposure-based, not observed-adoption experiments. Remote work, education, pre-trends, other simultaneous shocks and sample selection remain live attribution problems.
The Norwegian study is population-wide but Norway-specific; it relies on mapped occupational exposure rather than observed adoption and has only a short post-ChatGPT window through March 2025.
Broad firm-level results can hide occupational reallocation, hiring-path changes, pay effects and later consequences. Employment, hires, postings, earnings, hours and task use can move differently.
freshness_note: Updated 16 September 2026 after a Norwegian population-register counter-signal and a broader European firm-adoption result. We will revise when comparable studies observe adoption and track early hiring, pay and employment across countries.
